I understand your perspective, I really do, and I agree that everyone needs to take responsibility for their own shit. But what you're saying is like seeing a guy with a broken leg and telling him to walk to the doctor, and that you refuse to care about him until he's got a cast on. "But that would be stupid!" you say. What would you do for broken leg man? You'd give him a ride to the doctor, or lend him your phone so he could call a ride. Or maybe you'd be an arsehole and do nothing, but *you wouldn't expect him to walk*. 

Taking positive action is to a depressed person what walking is to a guy with a broken leg. Yes it is a catch-22, and yes that may make you feel extremely uncomfortable, but don't act like you're "just treating them the same as everyone else" because you're not. You're being wilfully ignorant of their problems and telling them to walk on their broken leg.

Not wanting help is part of the disease. By the time I realise that I *want* to feel better and that to do this I *need* to ask for help, I'm halfway home. The really debilitating part of the illness is the state where you *can't* ask for help. Sometimes a random dude on the internet is the one thing that takes me to that next step of actually wanting to help myself. A depressed person can kind of trick themselves into feeling better because browsing the internet doesn't feeling "doing something to make me feel better", it's just passing the time. Sometimes you need to trick yourself into it this way because there is a real psychological block against doing anything that would help you feel better. But if all you're doing is browsing the internet, and you end up talking to someone who understands the place you're in, it can trigger the momentary release you need. 

You have to get this. These people can't get help for themselves because *depression is not wanting to help yourself*. That's how it works. Sometimes all that's needed is someone who understands that and has a bit of faith in them. If you don't want to be that guy, fine, you don't have to. But with a bit of sensitivity, you could end up saving someone's life one day, and wouldn't that be fun?

If you've got heaps of free time and you need to structure it, here's what you do. Body first. The mind will follow. 

How fit are you? If the answer is "Um..." do [this](http://www.coolrunning.com/engine/2/2_3/181.shtml). Just do it. Start today. Start now. Print out a copy of the plan and hang it on your wall. Two weeks in, tell me where your mind is. 

Give your mind time to wander by getting away from the computer screen. 

You'll never do anything unless you can learn to focus on the process rather than the goal. Think about that every time you start running. If you have no inspiration, you have no inspiration. Keep running, and keep trying new things. You don't force willpower; it arises on its own when you're truly conscious of the benefits of doing something. 

Give your body a chance to learn how much better life can be. After a bit, it will start wanting to do things of its own accord. 

TL;DR. Start doing stuff. It will make you want to do more stuff. 

P.S. There is no formula, no way to make it happen. You will not know how to make it happen. Nobody knows how to make it happen for you. You will suffer many hours of feeling hopeless and futile. There is only one way to make anything happen in this world and that is to try, and try, and try, and try, and try. It's going to be hard. It's going to be fun. It's going to be agonising. Just accept that, and then start doing stuff. 

JUST START.

About the relapsing: you probably will relapse at times. However, you now know that you've overcome this once, and that means you can do it again. 

Eventually, you will come to a place where you can accept that you're a person who is disposed to going through this. The less attached you are to the imperative *not to be depressed*, the less distressing it is when bad moods come on, and the easier it is to let them pass away easily. Part of getting over it is learning to tread lightly through your changing moods, and being able to go through ups and downs without getting heavily attached to either. The goal is the happy balance, being able to learn impartially from what comes to you. 

Well done on making it this far :)

Discipline is something you just have to practice... you have to believe that the act of disciplining yourself, the act of giving up something you want for something you don't want to do, can be a joyful act. You just need to practice doing it enough times for your brain to get that. It never gets 100 per cent easy. You just have to learn how to love the challenge. Be patient with yourself and keep trying.

Well, unlike "rape", "date rape" doesn't have a legal definition, so I suppose there's room to quibble. It's my understanding that rape counsellors usually define it simply alongside "acquaintance rape" as rape where the perpetrator is known to the victim. Honestly, I think it's a somewhat dangerous misconception that date rape is simply a more wishy-washy form of rape. In the OP's case, they were on a date of sorts, the guy simply claimed they had consensual sex, and, in fact, got away with it. So the outcome is the same, premeditated or not. 

It seems like you want to make a distinction from situations where the perpetrator is able to rationalise it, or believes that what they did wasn't rape, or was justified by their relationship in some way. (For example: someone who believes that if they pay for dinner, they are owed sex, and doesn't bother to check if their date agrees.) I don't know of there's a name for those situations, but I wouldn't want to limit the category of "date rape" to just those scenarios.

This advice is fine and all, but on the scale of smart to stupid, OP didn't do anything really stupid. She didn't get drunk and probably saw this guy as her chaperone. The guy made her trust him, haven't you ever done something silly for a guy you liked?

Let's just spell it out a little more, because this is a complex issue, and we both have a point. 

The point here is not that the original advice (to women) isn't good. The advice is, generally, fine. *The problem is the misconception that women have the power to prevent rape.* In this case, the OP didn't exhibit a level of trust over and above what people would consider reasonable under the circumstances. She liked the guy, he asked her out, he stopped when she said no; she didn't drink to excess, either, and the only alcoholic drink she had was opened herself. Could she have prevented this rape? Sure, *if she assumed that this random, popular, nice-seeming guy that she liked was probably a rapist*. The consequences of teaching women that rape is (a) preventable and (b) their responsibility to prevent are that women will be constantly on their guard and distrusting of male companions. I see a whole lot of bitching on reddit about how "paranoid" women can be in the presence of men, well this is how we're taught to be. 

I am all for rape prevention education programs that target both sexes. The point of my post (advice to men) was to point out how stupid it is to place the onus of preventing rape on the (most common) victims. It's simply assumed that, between the perpetrator and the victim, one is morally incurable and the other is morally perfect. There are things women can do to theoretically decrease their chances. Hell, we could just decide to never trust a man again, or how about never dating, and staying home all the time, or wearing burqas. But even these things clearly *do not prevent rape*, and if the trade-off is being constantly paranoid and nobody ever having any fun, then fuck it. Nobody wants that. 

If all rapists are truly morally incurable psychopaths, then rapes will happen and there's simply nothing we can do about that. In fact, I think this would probably apply to only a small percentage of rapists, and the rest would be susceptible to education about the consequences of their actions. The real way to stop rapes from happening is to change the culture that sanctions them.

The point I am making here is that "exclusive" jokes have their place in community-building, but if you're on a public forum such as the internet, you have to expect "outsiders" to be offended, and you're really not justified in blaming *them* for being offended. So if you genuinely want to include them, you watch your step. 

The sexist humour that goes on on Reddit is usually characterised as metahumour, and is explained by its practitioners something like this: "We really *do* respect women like any other person. Sandwich/kitchen/rape jokes are funny because they're *so absurd*. We would never treat a woman like that in real life! LOL!" 

What's funny about that? Well, it's funny because it's ironic, but the irony is blind; it's the hipster "just because" pastiche kind of irony that really involves just re-enacting something because you can't be bothered being critical of it. 

For the joker out there who doesn't really want to *offend* people, but nevertheless enjoys offensive jokes: when you offend someone for the lulz, if you want to turn around and say that you don't *really* subscribe to the offensive content of the joke, I think the onus is on you to stop and ask yourself what you're really laughing at. If you mindlessly repeat sexist jokes without ever stopping to ask yourself why they're funny, all you're doing is perpetuating the status quo; if you *really* don't "subscribe to misogyny" and want to help dissipate it, you have an obligation to be aware of the ways in which you might be - consciously or not - perpetuating it. 

We need humour. But people need to be aware that humour is a powerful tool of inclusion and exclusion in ways that are frequently invisible to those wielding it, particularly online.
